 Order

The petitioners are accused nos. 1 to 5 in C.C. no. 242/2022 on the file of the Court of Judicial Magistrate First Class - IV, Kozhikode, which has originated from Crime no.649/2021 registered by the Nadakkavu Police Station, Kozhikode, alleging the commission of offences punishable under Sections 420 and 417 r/w Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code.

sentences.text:
2. The gist of the prosecution case is that, the accused persons, in furtherance of their common intention, started an establishment named "I Trust Human Rights and Welfare" and thereafter,
induced the public to believe that their establishment is an authorised organisation and received money from the public on the assurance of settling the disputes, despite 2026:KER:11000 not being a recognised statutory organisation.

entities.text: I Trust Human Rights and Welfare
entities.label: ORG

sentences.text: Thus, the accused have committed the above offences.
3. I have heard the learned counsel for the petitioner and the learned public prosecutor.

4. The learned counsel for the petitioners submit that, even if the allegations in Annexure A1 FIR and Annexure A2 final report are taken at their face value, the same would not constitute the offences alleged against the petitioners.
There is no material on the part of the prosecution to prove that the accused have received the money from the public.
The petitioners are the members of a registered trust, which is evidenced by Annexure A3 trust deed.

Other than for the mere allegation that the petitioners received money from the public, on the assurance of re-solving the disputes,
there is no material to prove their culpability in the crime.
Therefore, even if the petitioners face trial, it is not going to lead to a conviction.
Hence, the proceedings may be quashed.
The learned Public Prosecutor seriously opposes Crl.M.C.
He submits that there are specific allegations made against the petitioners in Annexure A1 FIR.
If the said allegations are taken at their face value, the same would constitute offences alleged against the petitioners.
The petitioners had impersonated themselves as the members of the State Human Rights Commission.

Accordingly,
they received money from the public, making them believe that the petitioners were authorised under law to settle disputes between the parties.
The fact that the petitioners received money from public by making them believe that they are an authorised agency is sufficient to prima facie establish mens rea on the part of the petitioners.
Hence, the Crl.M.C may be dismissed.

3 6.

The crux of the prosecution allegation is that, the petitioners, in furtherance of their common intentions, received money from the public by making them believe that they were members of the State 2026:KER:11000 Human Rights Commission.

7. It is well-settled that this Court has broad plenary powers under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which corresponds to Section 528 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita,
2023, to quash criminal proceedings.
However, such inherent power, though expansive in nature, is not unbridled or unlimited.
They are to be exercised sparingly, with circumspection, and within the parameters delineated by judicial precedents.

One of the elementary principles to quash a criminal proceeding is that, even if allegations in the first information report or the complaint are taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety, the same will not prima facie constitute any offence or make out a case against the accused.

(Read the decisions in State of Haryana and others v. Bhajan Lal and others [(1992) Supp (1) SCC 335], Central Bureau of Investigation v. Aryan Singh and Others [(2023) 18 SCC 399], Daxaben v. State of Gujarat and Others [(2022) 16 2026:KER:11000 SCC 117] and Monica Kumar and Another v. State of U.P. and Others [(2008) 8 SCC 781]).
8.

sentences.text: The Hon'ble Supreme Court has also consistently cautioned that High Courts, while exercising jurisdiction under Section 482 of the Code, should not embark upon a "minitrial" or weigh the sufficiency of evidence, which falls within the domain of the Trial Court.
The scope of enquiry is confined to whether, on a plain reading of the FIR/complaint and accompanying material, the ingredients of the alleged offence are disclosed.

(Read the decisions in Rajiv Thapar and others v.
Madal Lal Kapoor [(2013) 3 SCC 330] and HMT Watches Ltd. v. Abida M.A. and another [(2015) 11 SCC 776]).
9.

sentences.text: After carefully going through the allegations in Annexure A1 FIR and Annexure A2 final report, I find that there are specific allegations attributed against the petitioner that they received money from the public on the assurance of adjudicating the disputes between them 2026:KER:11000 and making them believe that the petitioners were members of the State Human Rights Commission.

10. In light of the specific allegations in a complaint, which prima facie constitute the offences alleged against the petitioners, I am not satisfied that this is a fit case to exercise the inherent powers of this Court under Section 528 of the BNSS.

In the aforesaid circumstances, I dismiss the Crl.M.C, but by reserving the right of the petitioners to raise all their contentions before the Trial Court, including filing an application for discharge, if the charge has not been framed till date.
If such an application is filed, the Trial Court is directed to consider and dispose of the application in accordance with law.
